title: OWASP Top 10 and secure coding
subtitle: The few web security bugs that cause most damage, and the plain coding habits that stop them.

c.v: On 8 March 2017, a US government security team publicly warned about a flaw in Apache Struts. Struts is a widely used, open-source framework for web apps. The flaw let an attacker run commands on the server.

Two days later, someone scanned Equifax's systems for it. They found an online dispute portal still running the old version, broke in, and confirmed they could run commands. They took no data that time.
Equifax did send the warning to its system administrators. But the list of people was out of date, so the people who should install the patch never got it. A scan a week later also missed the flaw.

From 13 May 2017, attackers used the portal again. They found a store of usernames and passwords kept unencrypted. With those, they reached 48 more databases. They ran about 9,000 queries, far more than normal work needs, and nothing limited them.

A device that inspected network traffic should have seen this. But its digital certificate had expired about 10 months before the breach, so it was not inspecting encrypted traffic. On 29 July 2017, an administrator replaced the certificate and saw the attack. It had lasted about 76 days. The attackers reached personal data of at least 145.5 million people in the US.
One unpatched framework let them in. Plain-text passwords, databases that were not separated and blind monitoring did the rest. This lesson covers the habits that stop each of these.
The OWASP Top 10 is "a standard awareness document" about the most critical security risks to web applications.
Treat it as a list of bug types to learn, not a full checklist.
, the eighth one. For it, OWASP used data from over 2.8 million applications. Eight categories come from testing data and two from a survey of practitioners.
Two changes since 2021 matter for daily work.
is now part of A01. A03 grows the old "Vulnerable and Outdated Components" to cover builds and distribution too.

Many of these bugs happen when your code trusts something it should not: user input, a library, a default setting or its own network. Check on the server, keep data apart from code, and give each part the least power it needs.

# Wrong: input becomes part of the SQL

# Right: a placeholder, so the driver passes input only as a value

c.v: Placeholders cannot hold table or column names. For a "sort by" field, map the user's choice to a fixed list of allowed names.
Also, never give your app's database account admin rights.

At Equifax, an expired certificate left a traffic monitor misconfigured, so it missed the attack.

build each environment from a script, with the same hardened settings everywhere and different credentials in each. Remove features and samples you do not use. Add one central setting that stops detailed error messages from reaching users.
Your app is mostly other people's code. You are exposed if you do not know every version you run, including dependencies of dependencies, or you do not scan them regularly.
OWASP lists a 2017 Apache Struts 2 flaw, CVE-2017-5638, and Log4Shell among its example attacks.

A tool like Dependabot compares your dependency list with a database of known flaws. It alerts you when a new flaw is published for a version you use.

if you know the target hosts, use an allow-list. Do not accept full URLs from users, and turn off redirects. If you must call any address, block private, loopback and link-local ranges and metadata endpoints. Check the address the name resolves to, and connect only to that address.
"Without logging and monitoring, attacks and breaches cannot be detected."
A common gap is logging only successful logins, so failed attempts go unseen.

log security events, including failures, with enough user context. Encode log data so attackers cannot inject fake lines. Keep personal data and secrets out of logs, and set alerts that people act on.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: In review, ask of every new endpoint:
"Who may call this, and where do we check it?"
for string-built SQL, shell commands and HTML. Each one needs a parameter, an argument list or an encoder.
For any feature that fetches a URL, ask:
Write the answer as an allow-list.
Keep dependency alerts at zero open critical items. Agree on a patch
with your team, and track it like a bug.
Give each service its own database user with only the tables it needs.
Check that failed logins and access denials are logged and alerted. Ask:
"Would we notice this attack within a day?"
Treat certificates, keys and secrets as things that expire. Put their dates in monitoring.
"Find every place in this repo that builds SQL, shell commands or HTML with string concatenation or f-strings. For each, show the safe version."
"List every endpoint that fetches a URL given by the user. For each, say which hosts it can reach, and whether it follows redirects."
"Scan the repo and its history for hard-coded secrets. List each one with file and commit, but do not print the secret."
Every query uses placeholders. Table and column names come from a fixed list.
An AI agent may add packages to fix a problem. Check that each new package is real, maintained and pinned, and that it shows up in your scanner.
No secret appears in code, test fixtures, prompts or logs that the agent wrote.
New handlers have the ownership check, not only the login check.
Read the agent's SSRF fix. A check on the host name alone is not enough. It must check the resolved address and connect to that same address.

options.v: Remove quote characters from the email before building the string.
Use a parameterized query, so the email is sent as a value, apart from the SQL.
Check the email format in the browser before it is sent.

why.v: OWASP's first defense is prepared statements with parameterized queries. The database then always tells code and data apart. OWASP calls escaping fragile, and browser checks can be skipped.

q.v: An endpoint downloads an image from any URL the user gives. What is the main risk?

options.v: Server-side request forgery. The server can be made to call internal addresses, like a cloud metadata endpoint.
Cross-site scripting in the user's browser.
The image might be too large.

why.v: SSRF abuses your server to reach the internal network or the machine itself. OWASP lists blocking metadata endpoints such as 169.254.169.254 among the defenses.

q.v: In the 2017 Equifax breach, why did the patch for the Apache Struts flaw not reach the dispute portal?

options.v: The patch did not exist yet.
The warning went to an out-of-date list, and a later scan missed the flaw.
The portal was written in a different language.

why.v: GAO reports that the recipient list was out of date, so the people who should patch never got the notice. A scan a week later did not find the flaw.

q.v: Which statement about input validation is true?

options.v: It is the main defense against SQL injection and XSS.
A deny-list of bad strings is safer than an allow-list.
It is useful, but you still need parameterized queries and output encoding.

why.v: OWASP separates validation from the defenses you need when you use the data. Use allow-lists on the server, plus parameterized queries for SQL and output encoding for HTML.

q.v: A teammate commits an API key to a public repo, then deletes it in the next commit. What should happen first?

options.v: Nothing. The key is gone now.
Revoke and rotate the key, then remove it from the code and logs.

why.v: OWASP's leak steps are revoke, rotate, then delete from the exposed system. The old commit still holds the key.
